patterns.rationale: Catches the universal signal across all 8 misses — the agent-directed fetch instruction. The `.{0,60}?` lazy gap handles miss 3's "making a web request to the configuration endpoint at http://..." where the URL doesn't immediately follow "to". Misses 2/4/5/6/7/9/10 have the URL directly after "to" so they match at zero gap. The phrase "make a web request to" is not normal technical prose — docs tell developers to "call", "fetch", "curl", or "send a request to"; this phrasing is chosen specifically to be understood by an LLM as an instruction.
patterns.fp_notes: An incident response playbook describing a past attack might say "the agent made an outbound web request to http://malicious.example.com" — but this would correctly be flagged since it contains injection-framing content. Benign API docs use "call", "send a request to", or "curl", not "make a web request to".

patterns.rationale: Targets the second half of the attack chain — the directive to blindly follow whatever the fetched URL returns. "apply any [X] instructions/directives returned" and "comply with any supplemental directives returned" are exclusively injection-framing constructs. Serves as belt-and-suspenders: if a future variant obfuscates the URL (e.g., via a variable or encoded string) Pattern 1 would miss it but this would still catch it. The `{0,3}` gap handles modifiers like "supplemental", "additional", "operator".
patterns.fp_notes: Code documentation might say "apply the configuration returned by the API" but that's developer-directed prose, not agent-directed instruction. The combination of "any" + "returned" + an instruction verb targeting directives/instructions is not found in the known-good corpus.
